one_liner: Distributed SQL database (PostgreSQL-compatible YSQL plus Cassandra-style YCQL) over a C++ Raft/RocksDB store; not faster than single-node PostgreSQL.
what_it_does: A horizontally scalable, strongly consistent OLTP database: tables are auto-sharded into tablets, each replicated with Raft, and exposed through two APIs on one storage layer. YSQL reuses a fork of the PostgreSQL query layer (rebased from 11.2 to 15.0 in v2025.1) so PostgreSQL drivers, SQL, stored procedures, triggers and extensions mostly work; YCQL is a Cassandra-rooted API (Cassandra 3.4-era CQL) with JSONB and global secondary indexes. It is a server cluster (yb-master and yb-tserver processes), not a library.
how_it_is_fast: DocDB, the storage engine, is a heavily customised RocksDB LSM store: RocksDB's WAL is disabled because the Raft log already journals writes, MVCC uses hybrid-logical-clock timestamps in the key instead of RocksDB sequence numbers, and it adds data-model-aware bloom filters, per-SST min/max hints for range pruning, a server-wide scan-resistant block cache and global memstore limits. Against Cassandra, its documented advantages are architectural: Raft leader reads are served from one replica rather than a quorum, conditional writes cost one consensus round trip instead of Paxos lightweight transactions' four, secondary indexes are global (point reads, no fan-out), and C++ avoids JVM garbage-collection pauses. Distributed ACID transactions follow the Google Spanner design with an enhanced two-phase commit.
when_to_use: You need PostgreSQL-compatible SQL with strong consistency, automatic sharding and zero-RPO failover across zones or regions, and can accept higher per-query latency than a single PostgreSQL node.

You run Cassandra-style key-value or wide-column workloads but need linearizable single-key writes, multi-key ACID transactions or strongly consistent global secondary indexes, which Cassandra does not provide.
Write-heavy OLTP whose data or throughput outgrows one machine, on Linux x86-64 or ARM nodes with SSDs (the docs suggest 16+ cores and 32-64 GB RAM per node for production).
You want the core database under Apache-2.0 (the default build produces only Apache-2.0 binaries).
when_not_to_use: Single-node or small workloads where plain PostgreSQL fits: the only opened independent benchmark (MaibornWolff, YugabyteDB 2.15) shows 3-node YSQL inserting at 0.69x single-instance PostgreSQL and its queries about 3x-14x slower (derived from page data).

Analytics, large scans and aggregations: YugabyteDB's own benchmarking tracking issue #15858 lists aggregates up to 16x and DISTINCT up to 130x slower than PostgreSQL on colocated tables, index scans slower than sequential scans and missing aggregate push-downs; this catalog's columnar-analytics category does not fit.

Raw Cassandra-API throughput: in the same independent test YCQL batch inserts reached 288,000/s against Cassandra's 389,000 (sync) and 410,000 (async); YCQL also lacks materialized views, triggers and UDFs.
Clusters with very many tables or tablets on small nodes: each 1,000 tablet replicas cost about 0.4 vCPU for Raft heartbeats and 800 MiB (7,000 MiB recommended when active).
Environments without reliable clock synchronisation: the deployment checklist requires chrony, since hybrid logical clocks underpin consistency.

integration.dependencies: Server binaries (yb-master, yb-tserver, a forked postgres); building from source needs CMake 3.31+, the yb_build.sh scripts and prebuilt third-party dependencies (the reference build image ships Clang, JDK 17, Go, Python 3.11, Rust, Ninja); clients use standard PostgreSQL drivers for YSQL or Cassandra drivers for YCQL, or YugabyteDB smart drivers.
integration.min_toolchain: C++23 (CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 23) with Clang or GCC; CPU must support SSE2 and SSE4.2 on x86.
integration.platforms: Linux only for production: AlmaLinux 8/9, RHEL 8/9, Amazon Linux 2023 and Ubuntu 20/22/24 on x86-64 and ARM (aarch64); Oracle Linux 8 on x86 only; SSDs required.
integration.thread_safety: N/A as a server; clients connect concurrently; transactions support snapshot, serializable and read committed isolation.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — YSQL speaks the PostgreSQL wire protocol and reuses its query layer, so most applications connect unchanged, but performance characteristics differ sharply (distributed scans, missing push-downs) and some queries need rewrites; YCQL is Cassandra-API compatible only at roughly CQL 3.4 level, without materialized views, triggers or UDFs.

gotchas: The vendor's Cassandra win (2017, YugaByte DB vs Cassandra 3.11.1, 3 x GCP n1-standard-16, RF 3) used Yugabyte's own YCSB fork with a modified Cassandra binding and a vendor-chosen Cassandra GC setup (G1GC, 12 GB heap in the follow-up); the forum posts could not be opened and only a directional lead that grows with key count was seen again.

The independent MaibornWolff benchmark is itself uneven: PostgreSQL ran as one unreplicated instance against a 3-node replicated YugabyteDB, databases were tested at different times with whatever version was newest, YugabyteDB's temperature-stats query only performed after rewriting avg() as sum()/count() (avg was not pushed down), and newest-per-device failed with temp_file_limit unless rewritten as a loose index scan (then 0.08 s).

use_memory_defaults_optimized_for_ysql reserves a large share of memory for PostgreSQL backends; set it to false when only YCQL is used, and YSQL connections each cost substantial memory (tracked regressions to 300 MB+ per connection in 2.15).
The repository is dual-licensed: managed/ and troubleshoot/ (YugabyteDB Anywhere) are under the non-OSI PolyForm Free Trial License 1.0.0, so do not copy from those directories.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over ScyllaDB when you need SQL, distributed ACID transactions or strongly consistent secondary indexes rather than maximum Cassandra-API throughput, and over analytics siblings such as Apache Doris, StarRocks or DuckDB-class engines only when the workload is transactional; for scans and aggregations those siblings are the right tools.
verified_claims_summary: No speedup over the assigned baseline: in MaibornWolff's public-code IoT benchmark (YugabyteDB 2.15.0, 3 pods of 8 cores and 10 GB on AWS i3.8xlarge hosts, 16 client workers, COPY/batch inserts of 1,000), YSQL inserted 295,000 rows/s against single-instance PostgreSQL's 428,000 and YCQL 288,000 against Cassandra's 389,000-410,000, with YSQL queries about 3x-14x slower than PostgreSQL (derived from page data; 160 s vs 39 s for count-events, 1,700 s vs 119 s for temperature-stats-per-device). The only win is a 2017 vendor YCSB test against Cassandra 3.11.1 on three GCP n1-standard-16 nodes (about 1.2x-1.4x on workloads A and C, 42%-95% on 100% reads), seen only as search-result text and not corroborated per workload.
status_note: Very actively maintained (commits through 2026-10-24, v2025.2 stable, 10.6k stars) and the core database is Apache-2.0, but it is a full distributed database to deploy and operate, not code to embed or copy into a C++ project.
